edges.effect_quant: Dietary strategies aimed at lowering inflammation may reduce some forms of endometriosis pain, but the evidence is mixed and intervention-specific. A 2024 meta-analysis of randomized dietary trials found antioxidant supplementation reduced dysmenorrhea (MD -1.95, 95% CI -3.78 to -0.13) but did not clearly improve chronic pelvic pain. A recent omega-3 cohort also reported greater odds of clinically meaningful pain reduction (OR 3.06, 95% CI 1.85 to 5.06), while a 2025 omega-3 meta-analysis found no clear pooled pain effect.
edges.population: women with confirmed endometriosis using anti-inflammatory or exclusion-style dietary interventions as adjunctive symptom management
edges.mechanism: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory condition, so diets or supplements that lower pro-inflammatory signaling could plausibly reduce cytokine-driven nociception and pelvic pain. Benefits may vary by nutrient composition, adherence, gut sensitivity, and baseline inflammatory phenotype.
edges.summary: The evidence leans protective but is still early and uneven. Some dietary interventions, especially selected supplements or targeted exclusion diets, appear to improve dysmenorrhea or global pain in subsets of patients, yet pooled trial evidence remains heterogeneous enough that a modest, cautious interpretation is the most defensible.
edges.caveats: This edge should not be read as proof that one universal anti-inflammatory diet reliably treats endometriosis pain. Trials are small, heterogeneous, and often combine supplements with broader dietary advice, so the current signal is promising but not definitive.
